title: The Aral Sea: Lessons from a Disappearing Lake
paragraphs: Until the 1960s, the Aral Sea, which lies on the border between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was the fourth largest lake in the world. It covered an area of about 68,000 square kilometres and supported a large fishing industry. The towns of Aral and Muynak were busy ports, and the fish caught in the lake were sent to markets across the Soviet Union. The lake was fed by two great rivers, the Amu Darya in the south and the Syr Darya in the north, which carried water from the mountains of Central Asia.

The decline of the sea began with a political decision. In the 1960s, Soviet planners decided to turn the dry plains of Central Asia into a major centre of cotton production. To do this, they built thousands of kilometres of canals that took water from the two rivers and delivered it to the fields. The plan was successful in terms of cotton: the region became one of the largest producers in the world. However, many of the canals were poorly built, and a large proportion of the water was lost through evaporation and leaks before it reached the crops.

The effect on the lake was dramatic. With much less water flowing in, the sea began to shrink. By the 1990s, it had divided into two separate bodies of water, and by 2014 the eastern part of the southern sea had dried up completely. As the water disappeared, the remaining lake became much saltier, and most of the fish species died. The fishing industry collapsed, and thousands of people lost their jobs. Former ports now stand many kilometres from the water, and rusting ships lie in the sand of what is now called the Aralkum Desert.

The consequences have not been limited to the economy. The dry seabed is covered with salt, as well as chemicals from fertilisers that were washed into the rivers over many decades. Strong winds carry this dust across the region, sometimes for hundreds of kilometres. Researchers have linked the dust to an increase in respiratory illnesses among people living nearby. The loss of the lake has also changed the local climate: summers have become hotter and winters colder, because the large body of water no longer moderates the temperature.

Not all of the news is bad, however. In 2005, with support from the World Bank, Kazakhstan completed the Kokaral Dam, which separates the smaller northern part of the sea from the southern part. The dam keeps the water of the Syr Darya in the north, and the results have been better than many experts expected. The water level of the North Aral Sea has risen by several metres, the salt content has fallen, and fish have returned. Local fishermen are working again, and some families who had left the area have come back.

The southern sea, by contrast, is unlikely to recover in the near future, because the Amu Darya is still used heavily for agriculture. Instead, Uzbekistan has focused on reducing the harm caused by the dry seabed. Since 2018, millions of salt-tolerant plants, such as saxaul shrubs, have been planted across the former lake floor to hold the soil and reduce dust storms. The story of the Aral Sea is often described as one of the worst environmental disasters of the twentieth century, but it also shows that careful management can repair at least part of the damage.

questionGroups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Choose TRUE if the statement agrees with the information, FALSE if the statement contradicts the information, or NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

questions.explanation: The passage says it was the fourth largest lake in the world, but does not compare it with other lakes in Central Asia.
questions.statement: Before the 1960s, the Aral Sea was the largest lake in Central Asia.

questions.explanation: Paragraph B: a large proportion of the water was lost through evaporation and leaks.
questions.statement: The canals built by Soviet planners lost a lot of water before it reached the fields.

questions.explanation: Paragraph C: only the eastern part of the southern sea had dried up completely.
questions.statement: By 2014, the whole of the southern sea had disappeared.

questions.explanation: Paragraph D: the seabed is covered with salt and chemicals from fertilisers.
questions.statement: Dust from the dry seabed contains chemicals from farming.

questions.explanation: The passage mentions World Bank support but says nothing about the cost.
questions.statement: The Kokaral Dam cost more than the World Bank had planned.
